choices.text: A heron spears a frog and swallows it
choices.rationale: Correct: the heron benefits by eating the frog, which is classic predation.

choices.text: Fleas drink a kitten's blood while living in its fur
choices.rationale: This is parasitism: the fleas live on a living host and take a little blood at a time instead of eating the kitten.

questions.prompt: An African savanna and a northern forest share no species. Why can scientists use what they learned about lions and zebras to predict how wolves and moose will affect each other?
questions.accessiblePrompt: An African savanna and a northern forest share no species. Why can scientists use what they learned about lions and zebras to predict how wolves and moose will affect each other?
questions.limitations: A shared pattern supports a likely prediction, not a guarantee; local factors such as weather, food plants and disease still matter.

choices.text: Predator-prey interactions follow similar patterns across ecosystems
choices.rationale: Correct: the species differ, but the cause-and-effect pattern between a predator population and its prey repeats in ecosystems around the world.

choices.text: Wolves and lions are the same species, so they hunt in the same way
choices.rationale: Wolves belong to the dog family and lions are big cats; the prediction rests on a shared pattern, not a shared species.

choices.text: Every ecosystem holds exactly the same number of predators and prey
choices.rationale: Ecosystems hold very different numbers of predators and prey; what repeats is how the two populations affect each other.

choices.text: The two places share the same weather, so their animals behave alike
choices.rationale: A hot savanna and a cold northern forest have very different weather, yet the pattern holds in both.

questions.explanation: Interaction patterns repeat even when the species change. Lions and zebras, wolves and moose, and stray cats and mice are different animals in different places, but in each pair plenty of prey feeds more predators, and more predators eat the prey down. That shared pattern lets scientists predict what is likely to happen in an ecosystem with species they haven't studied as closely.
questions.misconception: What scientists learn about one ecosystem can't help them in an ecosystem with different species.
questions.hint: Compare the role each animal plays in its own ecosystem, not the animals themselves.

evidence.supports: The species that fill predator roles differ between ecosystems, but feeding patterns are similar, so scientists can predict a population's changes from its feeding relationships.
Scientists see the same rise-and-fall pattern between carnivore and prey populations all over the world.
Patterns in how interactions affect populations are found in ecosystems everywhere on Earth, which lets scientists predict and manage population changes.
